OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $\epsilon>0$ and $n$ be large depending on $\epsilon$. Is it true that for all $n^\epsilon<k\leq n^{1-\epsilon}$ the number of distinct prime divisors of $\binom{n}{k}$ is\[(1+o(1))k\sum_{k<p<n}\frac{1}{p}?\]Or perhaps even when $k \geq (\log n)^c$?
#685: [Er79d]
number theory | 
primes | 
binomial coefficients
It is trivial that the number of prime factors is\[>\frac{\log \binom{n}{k}}{\log n},\]and this inequality becomes (asymptotic) equality if $k>n^{1-o(1)}$.

 Up to lower order errors of $O(k)$, the number to be counted is the number of primes between $k$ and $n$ that divide an element of $(n-k,n]$, thanks to Kummer's formula. The problem is somewhat comparable to a prime number theorem for short intervals $[x,x+x^\varepsilon]$.

 A partial observation: combining Younis’ short-interval asymptotic for $\Psi(x+h,y)-\Psi(x,y)$ with the fact that for $k>\sqrt n$, $\omega_{>k}!\binom{n}{k}$ is exactly the number of non-$k$-smooth integers in $(n-k,n]$, seems to give
$\omega!\binom{n}{k}=(1+o_\delta(1)),k\sum_{k<p<n}\frac1p$ uniformly for $n^{17/30+\delta}\le k\le n^{1-\delta}$.
I have not been able to find this specific subrange written down explicitly in the literature or on this page.
So unless I am missing a reference, #685 appears to be settled at least in that upper range by existing smooth-number method.
